title: GLES3: Allocate transform feedback output buffers as GL_DYNAMIC_COPY
body:
The GLES3 renderer skins (and blends) on the GPU with transform feedback into a per-instance vertex buffer, `MeshInstance::Surface::vertex_buffers[]`, that draws then read. The CPU never writes those buffers, but they were allocated `GL_DYNAMIC_DRAW` (the on-demand motion-vector buffer followed the source surface's `USE_DYNAMIC_UPDATE` flag). This PR allocates all three as `GL_DYNAMIC_COPY`, the hint the GL spec gives for "modified repeatedly by GL, used as a source for GL drawing".

### Why it matters

On Windows, Compatibility runs through ANGLE's D3D11 backend on the GPUs Godot forces to ANGLE (and in every browser for the web export). ANGLE's D3D11 backend classifies `DYNAMIC_DRAW`/`STREAM_DRAW` as CPU-updated buffers (`BufferD3D::updateD3DBufferUsage`) and never binds such a buffer to the input assembler directly (`Buffer11::supportsDirectBinding()` is `usage == STATIC`). Every draw that reads a "dynamic" attribute re-streams it on the CPU (`VertexDataManager::storeDynamicAttribs` → `Buffer11::getData`), and because transform feedback marked the buffer written (`markTransformFeedbackUsage` → `invalidateStaticData`), `getData` first copies the GPU buffer back through a staging buffer with `Map(D3D11_MAP_READ)`. So every skinned body whose skeleton changed that frame costs a GPU readback and a CPU copy of its whole vertex buffer, per draw that reads it, and the buffer can never be promoted to static because the next frame's feedback pass writes it again.

All `*_COPY` and `*_READ` usages map to ANGLE's `STATIC` class, which binds the D3D11 buffer directly. The skinned layout (position `3 × float`, normal and tangent `2 × uint32` via `glVertexAttribIPointer`, 28-byte stride, 4-byte aligned offsets) needs no conversion, so `DirectStoragePossible` holds. Transform feedback already writes into ANGLE's `VERTEX_OR_TRANSFORM_FEEDBACK` D3D11 storage whatever the hint, so the draw now reads the same D3D11 buffer the feedback pass wrote.

### Measurements (Godot 4.7.2 stable, Compatibility, Windows 11, GTX 780, i7-4770K, 1360×768)

Same scene and camera, one hero plus 11 animated humanoid mobs and 3 NPCs (14 skinned bodies, 253 draws, 144k primitives), `RenderingServer.viewport_get_measured_render_time_cpu` per frame, each part measured by hiding it:

| | native GL (`opengl3`) | ANGLE D3D11 (`opengl3_angle`) |
|---|---|---|
| whole frame render CPU | 1.63 ms | 9.9–10.2 ms |
| the 11 mobs | ≈0.3 ms | 5.3–5.4 ms |
| same 11 mobs, skeletons frozen (meshes still skinned and bound) | | ≈0 ms |
| same 11 mobs drawn from their static mesh buffers (no skeleton) | | 0.1 ms |

About 0.45 ms per re-skinned body per frame on that CPU, nothing for a skinned body whose bones did not change, so the cost is exactly the per-draw re-stream plus readback of the feedback-written buffer described above. Draw count, primitive count and GPU load did not move it.

### Testing

I have not yet benchmarked a build with this patch on D3D11; the numbers above are from the stock 4.7.2 template and isolate the mechanism (frozen skeleton = no feedback write = no cost). The patch builds and I will post a before/after from the same box once I have a Windows template with it. Native GL drivers only take the hint as advisory, so no change is expected there.

Happy to split the motion-vector buffer change out if that line should keep following the surface's update flag.
